# Background & Motivation

\bluehead{1. Project background}

- During \textbf{COVID-19}, protective behaviours such as \textbf{mask wearing}, social distancing, hand hygiene, and self-isolation were important for reducing transmission.

\vspace{0.15cm}

- Compliance was shaped not only by policy rules, but also by risk perception, trust, demographic characteristics, wellbeing, and broader social context.

\vspace{0.15cm}

- These predictors may operate \textbf{differently across countries} because policy environments, institutions, culture, and public expectations vary (Ryan et al., 2025).











# Background & Motivation

\bluehead{2. Research questions}


- Within each country, do the key predictors of compliance with COVID-19 protective behaviours change before and after mask mandates?

- Are these changes consistent across countries, or do they vary?

- Is there a set of common cross-national predictors, alongside country-specific predictors?

# Data Sources

\bluehead{1. Behaviour and policy datasets}

\small
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{YouGov dataset:} repeated survey responses about people's COVID-19 behaviours, attitudes, and background characteristics (Imperial College London and YouGov, 2022).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Behaviour: whether people wore masks, kept physical distance, washed hands...
  \item Predictor: age group, gender, confidence in health services...
  \end{itemize}

\vspace{0.3cm}


\item \textbf{OxCGRT dataset:} This dataset contains the strictness with which the government has enforced its mask-wearing policy (Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker, 2023).
\vspace{0.3cm}

\item The two sources are linked by \textbf{country, region and survey date}.
\end{itemize}

# What Have I Done So Far?

\bluehead{1. Data pre-processing}

\vspace{0.25cm}

\begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}

\begin{itemize}
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35cm}
\item For the YouGov and OxCGRT files, various formatting issues have been resolved.
\item \textbf{ Mapped survey regions to policy regions}: Convert all place names in both datasets to lower-case English letters, then match them one-to-one.
\item \textbf{ Defined before/after mandate periods}.
\item \textbf{ Defined two outcomes}: Face-mask-wearing and Overall-protective-behaviour.
\item \textbf{ Cleaned the data}:  Removing columns and samples with too many missing values, encoding the data, making column names more readable, and splits.
\end{itemize}

\end{column}

\begin{column}{0.38\textwidth}

\end{columns}






# What Have I Done So Far?

\bluehead{2. About Model}
\vspace{0.25cm}

\setlength{\fboxsep}{7pt}
\setlength{\fboxrule}{0.6pt}

\fbox{
\begin{minipage}{0.92\textwidth}
\textbf{\textcolor{myblue}{Model 1: Random Forest}} \\
This model builds many decision trees and lets them vote for the final prediction. Capable of handling non-linearity.

\vspace{0.18cm}

\textbf{\textcolor{myblue}{Model 2: XGBoost}} \\
This model also uses decision trees, but it builds them step by step. Each new tree tries to correct the mistakes made by the previous trees. Capable of handling non-linearity.
\end{minipage}}

\vspace{0.28cm}

\fbox{
\begin{minipage}{0.92\textwidth}
\textbf{\textcolor{myblue}{Metric: AUC}} \\
AUC means Area Under the ROC Curve; selected because it can measure model separation across all classification thresholds. AUC ranges from 0 to 1. A higher AUC indicates better separation between compliant and non-compliant respondents.
\end{minipage}}

# Results

\bluehead{2. Train-test split}

The next step was to prepare data for modelling.

- I split the data separately for each country, policy period, and outcome.

- I used an 80/20 train-test split.

- Stratification (based on the outcome class, maintain a similar proportion of categories  in the train and test sets) was used where possible to preserve the class balance of the outcome.


\vspace{0.25cm}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Dimension & Values & Number \\
\midrule
Countries & AUS, BRA, CAN, GBR, IND, USA & 6 \\
Policy periods & Before mandate, after mandate & 2 \\
Outcomes & Face mask, overall protective behaviour & 2 \\
\midrule
Total modelling tasks & $6 \times 2 \times 2$ & 24 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

# Results

\bluehead{4. Feature importance}

\vspace{0.05cm}

\small
Feature importance indicates how much each predictor contributes to the model’s prediction. 
A higher importance score means that the factor plays a stronger role (Calculated after model training based on the contribution of each variable to the predicted results).

# Summary

\bluehead{Summary of main findings}


- \textbf{XGBoost }achieved the \textbf{best} or joint-best AUC in most modelling tasks, while Random Forest provided a useful comparison model with similar performance in some cases.

- The before/after comparison suggests that \textbf{ the predictors of compliance are not fixed}. Their importance changes after mask mandates, and the direction of change differs across countries.

- \textbf{Some predictors appear repeatedly across countries}, such as non-mask protective behaviour, willingness to self-isolate, survey timing, and confidence-related variables. Other predictors are more country-specific.
